name: Baraïn
catalog_citation: Lovestrand, Joseph. 2012. The Linguistic Structure of Baraïn (Chadic). MA thesis, Graduate Institute of Applied Linguistics (Dallas). PDF: https://www.diu.edu/documents/theses/
catalog_locator: Chapter 5 'Tone', opening paragraph, printed p.52 (PDF p.69); abstract; section 5.5 'Intonation' p.67
catalog_quote: Baraïn, like all known Chadic languages, is tonal (Newman 2006:193; Frajzyngier & Shay 2012:246). Three levels of tone are contrastive in the lexicon. No grammatical tone has been discovered other than the phrase-final effects described as intonation below (section 5.5). There is just one example in the data of a minimal triplet contrasting all three levels of tone. (99) [átːá] 'arm' [ātːá] '(number of) times' [àtːá] 'stomach' ... There is no predictable relationship between tone and vowel length or tone and voicing (i.e., no consonant-tone interference).

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the only grammar of Baraïn (Lovestrand 2012, 311 pp, dedicated tone chapter), which we hold; the deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited page (printed p.52 / PDF p.69) and the section 5.5 intonation quote at p.67. The author's later works (2018 DPhil fetched sources now from ORA; 2022 OUP book per Crossref chapter list) are morphosyntactic and restate that Barayin is tonal with low functional load, with no word-stress or accent claim anywhere. No independent phonology/prosody study of the language exists in Glottolog or the author's own bibliographies. Coding 'tonal, no stress rule stated, domain UNSTATED' stands; nothing to recode. tx

sources.citation: Lovestrand, Joseph. 2018. Serial verb constructions in Barayin: Typology, description and Lexical-Functional Grammar. DPhil thesis, University of Oxford. 326 pp. ORA uuid:39406562-02d3-46f5-abf3-180d22225925
sources.quote: p.74: 'Although Barayin is a tonal language, the functional load of contrastive tone is relatively low. Minimal pairs are relatively infrequent. ... In several places in the pronominal system, the second-person and third-person plural forms are distinguished by tone.' p.52: 'Chadic languages are tonal. There are often two contrastive levels of tone, sometimes three.' No mention of word stress or accent anywhere in the thesis (grep of full text: 'stress' only in an English focus-reading remark; 'prosody' only re SVC prosodic unity).
